items.title: 13.7 Relative reactivity of halide ions as reducing agents

blocks.text: The reducing ability of halide ions increases down the group from fluoride to iodide, mainly because electronegativity decreases and atomic radius increases, giving lower charge density and easier donation of an electron. Fluoride is the weakest and iodide the strongest reducing agent: I- > Br- > Cl- > F-. The high electronegativity of fluorine and the strong hold on its extra electron make it hard for F- to donate electrons, and the small size of F- gives a high charge density that further stabilises it. Chloride is a stronger reducing agent than fluoride but weaker than bromide and iodide, because of its larger size and lower electronegativity. Bromide is stronger than chloride: bromine is less electronegative, and Br- has a larger radius and lower charge density, so it loses an electron easily. Iodide is much stronger than both: iodine's electronegativity is much lower, and the large I- ion has a low charge density and a strong tendency to donate an electron.

blocks.prompt: F- is a weaker reducing agent than Cl-. Explain why (Quick Check 13.4a).
blocks.explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative element and the fluoride ion is tiny, so its extra electron is held very tightly close to the nucleus at high charge density; it is hard to remove. Chloride is larger and chlorine less electronegative, so its outer electron is held more loosely and is given up more readily, making Cl- the better reducing agent.

items: Reducing power I- > Br- > Cl- > F-: down the group electronegativity falls and radius grows, charge density falls, and the electron is donated more easily; the opposite of the X2 oxidising trend.
